title: New Electronic Skin Senses Ten Times More Than Current Prosthetic Sensors
excerpt: Washington State University researchers develop a 3D-printed e-skin that detects pressure and temperature at unprecedented resolution, laying the groundwork for bionic touch.
body:
• Washington State University researchers have developed an electronic skin that senses pressure and temperature at 10 times the resolution of existing commercial glove sensors.
  • The system uses a "scan-model-print" method with 3D printing and laser cutting, allowing modules to snap together and conform to any prosthetic limb shape.
  • Published in Cell Reports Physical Science, the work addresses a longstanding gap: current e-skins are expensive, poorly fitted, and lose accuracy when customized.
  • The team is now developing an actuator to convert the sensor signals into nerve stimulation, which could eventually let amputees feel what they touch.

Amputees may one day feel the warmth of a coffee cup or the texture of fabric through their prosthetic limbs. A research team at Washington State University has built an electronic skin that detects pressure and temperature at a scale 10 times finer than the commercial glove sensors currently available — a step that could make bionic touch practical for clinical use.

The work, published in the journal Cell Reports Physical Science in August 2026, was led by graduate student Hongyi Shen and Kaiyan Qiu, Berry Family Assistant Professor in WSU's School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering.

What Makes This E-Skin Different

Electronic skins already exist, but they come with significant trade-offs. They are expensive, cover only small areas, and tend to lose sensing accuracy the more they are shaped to fit a particular limb. The data they generate is also too large to process in real time.

"Often these devices are forced to compromise between comfort and mechanical reliability," Shen told TechXplore.

The WSU team tackled these problems with thin-layer sandwich modules that incorporate both temperature and pressure sensors. The modules snap together like Lego bricks — no adhesives required — and conform to the freeform shape of any prosthetic limb.

"This approach democratizes the production of medical-grade e-skins, making advanced tactile feedback viable for widespread clinical adoption."

— Hongyi Shen, first author and WSU graduate researcher

How the "Scan-Model-Print" Method Works

The researchers used a three-step manufacturing process. A scanner maps the geometry of a prosthetic. That shape is modeled digitally, then the sensors are 3D-printed and laser-cut to match.

"The scanner basically scans the prosthetic and then, based on the geometry, we map our sensors as a multimodal sensing system with that geometry," Qiu said. "This enables our sensing system to have seamless coverage over the freeform region on the prosthetics."

The result is a sensor array that measures both pressure and temperature at high density across flat or curved surfaces. It reliably identifies surface textures and material properties — capabilities that could help amputees perform everyday tasks with far greater confidence.

The Road to Bionic Touch

Sensing is only half the equation. The team has submitted a provisional patent and is now developing an actuator to convert the e-skin's electrical signals into stimulation that nearby nerves can interpret. If successful, amputees could receive real-time feedback about what they are touching.

"I think what we are doing in this project will someday help make amputees' lives easier with our device," Shen said.

What It Means for Prosthetics

The project was partially supported by WSU's National Science Foundation Research Traineeship in Next-Generation Robotics. Its relatively simple manufacturing — 3D printing and laser cutting — could keep costs low enough for widespread adoption, a persistent barrier in the field.

For India's prosthetics sector, which serves an estimated 2.2 million amputees according to government data, affordable and customizable e-skin technology could have significant implications. India's growing robotics and biomedical engineering programs are increasingly focused on assistive devices, and cost-effective manufacturing methods like the WSU approach align with the country's push for accessible healthcare technology.

The researchers say their next milestone is a fully integrated bionic skin with both sensing and haptic stimulation — a system where a prosthetic hand would not just grip an object, but tell its wearer exactly what it feels like.
